q: The black soil of the Deccan is formed from the weathering of:
options: the alluvium of the Godavari
the basaltic lava of the Deccan Trap
the laterite of the Western Ghats
the granite of the Peninsular plateau
explanation: The black soil or regur of the Deccan is derived from the weathering of the basaltic lava of the Deccan Trap, and it is also called the black cotton soil for its remarkable moisture retention.

q: The 'usar' or 'reh' lands of northern India are:
options: the peaty soils of Kerala
the black soils of the Deccan
saline and alkaline soils found in the semi-arid regions
the sandy soils of the Thar
explanation: The usar lands are the saline and alkaline soils of the semi-arid regions, called 'reh' in Rajasthan, 'kallar' in the Punjab and Uttar Pradesh and 'thor' in Gujarat, and they are reclaimed with the gypsum and the drainage.

q: The laterite soil of India is found in the areas of:
options: the arid regions of western Rajasthan
heavy rainfall and high temperature
low rainfall and a cold climate
the high altitude of the Himalayan ranges
explanation: Laterite is formed by the intense leaching of the soluble materials in the heavy rainfall and the high temperature regions, and it is rich in the iron and the aluminium oxides and is used as the building blocks in the coastal architecture.

q: The 'sheet', 'rill' and 'gully' are the successive stages of:
options: soil erosion by the running water
the denudation of the hills
the weathering of the rocks
the deposition of the alluvium
explanation: Sheet erosion removes the thin films of the topsoil, the rill erosion cuts the small channels and the gully erosion forms the deep channels that cannot be smoothed by the normal tillage, and all the three are the stages of the water erosion.

q: The 'shelter belts' and the 'wind breaks' are measures of:
options: the prevention of the soil erosion by the rivers
the improvement of the irrigation
the control of the desertification of the land
the prevention of the wind erosion and the conservation of the soil
explanation: The shelter belts and the wind breaks are lines of trees planted to check the wind velocity and to trap the moving sand, and they are an effective measure against the wind erosion and the desertification.

q: The 'tropical evergreen' forests of India occur mainly in:
options: the dry interior of Rajasthan
the high altitudes of Ladakh
the western deserts of Gujarat
the western coast, the north-east and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
explanation: The tropical evergreen forests grow where the rainfall exceeds 200 cm and the temperature is high throughout the year, and they are found on the western coast, in the north-east and in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

q: The 'teak' is the most characteristic species of the:
options: mangrove forests
montane coniferous forests
temperate grasslands
tropical deciduous forests
explanation: The teak is the dominant species of the tropical deciduous or the monsoon forests, which are the most widespread forest type in India and are found in the regions of a rainfall between 70 and 200 cm.

q: The 'babul', 'khejri' and 'cactus' are the typical species of the:
options: tropical deciduous forests
montane forests
tropical thorn forests
mangrove forests
explanation: The tropical thorn forests of the arid and the semi-arid regions of the west have the xerophytic species like the babool, the khejri, the cactus and the date palm, and they are the natural vegetation of the Thar and of the Rajasthan.

q: The 'Sundari' tree is associated with the:
options: the dry deciduous forests
mangrove forests
the tropical evergreen forests
the montane forests
explanation: The Sundari, the Rhizophora and the Ceriops are the characteristic species of the mangrove forests, which grow in the tidal mud of the estuaries and the deltas, and the Sundarban is the largest mangrove forest in the world.

q: The 'deodar', 'pine' and 'silver fir' are the species of the:
options: tropical thorn forests
the mangrove forests
montane forests
tropical deciduous forests
explanation: The montane or the temperate forests occur at a height of about 1,500 to 3,000 metres in the Himalayas and the western ghats and they yield the deodar, the pine, the silver fir, the oak and the cedar.

q: The alpine meadows of the higher Himalayas are locally called the:
options: Bugyal
Dhoop
Chaparral
Shola
explanation: The bugyals are the alpine meadows of the higher Himalayas of Ladakh and of the Spiti where the yaks and the sheep graze in the summer, and the shola is the scrub of the transitional zone below the tree line.

q: The 'Kharif' crops of India are:
options: grown only in the irrigated tracts of the Punjab
sown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in the September-October
sown in the winter and harvested in the spring
grown in the summer months between the rabi and the kharif
explanation: The kharif crops are sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon in the June-July and are harvested in the September-October, and the rice, the maize, the jowar, the bajra, the cotton and the jute are the principal kharif crops.

q: The 'Aus' season of rice cultivation is practised in:
options: Punjab
Kerala
Rajasthan
West Bengal
explanation: The aus or the autumn rice is the third rice crop of the year in the irrigated tracts of West Bengal, where the boro, the aman and the aus crops are grown in sequence on the same land.

q: The 'cropping intensity' of a region is:
options: the ratio of the irrigated area to the net sown area
the ratio of the gross cropped area to the net sown area
the ratio of the foodgrain production to the net sown area
the ratio of the area under the commercial crops to the total area
explanation: Cropping intensity equals the gross cropped area divided by the net sown area, so an intensity of 100 per cent means that the land is sown only once a year, and the multiple cropping raises it above 100 per cent.

q: The 'Ahar' system of cultivation is associated with:
options: the Tamil Nadu delta
the Konkan coast
Bihar and the eastern Uttar Pradesh
the Bundelkhand region
explanation: In the Ahar system of the eastern India the winter rice is sown in the monsoon season on the lowlands using the residual moisture and the wheat follows in the rabi, and the system is also known as the monsoon cropping.

q: The 'Zaid' season crops of India include:
options: rice and wheat
sugarcane and cotton
the millets and the oilseeds
watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and the fodder crops
explanation: The Zaid is the short summer season between the rabi and the kharif and the crops grown in it are the water melons, the muskmelons, the cucumbers and the fodder and the moong, and the irrigation is essential for them.

q: The 'Terai' belt is characterised by:
options: dense forest, marshy land and the numerous streams that disappear in the Bhabar
the coarse sandy soil of the arid west
the black soil of the river terraces
the laterite plateau of the peninsula
explanation: The Terai is the marshy belt of the alluvium south of the Bhabar where the streams reappear and the ground is wet and fertile, and the mithai or the sugarcane and the rice are the characteristic crops.

q: The 'rabi' crops of India are sown in the month of:
options: January and February
June and July
October and November
March and April
explanation: The rabi crops are sown in the cool season from the middle of October to the middle of November with the arrival of the winter rains and they are harvested in March and April.

q: The 'rabi' crop that covers the largest area in India is:
options: barley
gram
mustard
wheat
explanation: Wheat is the most important rabi crop and with the gram, the mustard and the barley it accounts for the bulk of the area sown in the winter across the Indo-Gangetic plain.

q: The 'Jute' is a fibre crop grown mainly in the states of:
options: West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and Odisha
Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Punjab and Haryana
Gujarat and Rajasthan
explanation: Jute, the golden fibre, needs the alluvial soil of the humid Bengal and the Brahmaputra valley, and West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya account for the bulk of the production.

q: The 'Tea' in India is grown in:
options: Odisha and Chhattisgarh
Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala
Punjab and Haryana
Rajasthan and Gujarat
explanation: The tea plantations need a warm and humid climate with a well distributed rainfall, and the major growing states are Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala with Karnataka and the Nilgiris also being important.

q: The 'Rubber' plantations in India are concentrated in:
options: Assam and Meghalaya
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Tripura
Punjab and Haryana
Rajasthan and Gujarat
explanation: Rubber is a tropical plantation crop of the humid equatorial climate and it is grown in the southern and the western ghats regions of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and in Tripura.

q: The 'Coffee' in India is mainly grown in:
options: Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Gujarat and Maharashtra
Assam and West Bengal
Punjab and Haryana
explanation: Coffee needs a mild climate with heavy rainfall and the shade of the trees, and the 'Coffee Board' records the bulk of the production in Karnataka followed by Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

q: The 'Apple' of India is grown in:
options: Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Rajasthan and Gujarat
West Bengal and Assam
Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand
explanation: The apple requires a cool and temperate climate with the chilling hours of the winter, and the orchards are concentrated in the higher hills of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

q: The 'pulses' in India are mainly grown as:
options: a cold season crop of the hill states
a summer crop of the coastal tracts
kharif crops in the rain fed areas
rabi crops in the irrigated areas
explanation: Most of the pulses like the tur, the urad, the moong and the moth are the kharif crops of the rain fed tracts, and the gram is the notable exception as it is a rabi crop.

q: The 'Sugarcane' in India is a:
options: a rabi crop sown in November
a cold season crop of the western plateau
a short duration kharif crop of four months
a long duration crop that occupies the fields for over a year
explanation: Sugarcane is a long duration crop that takes about a year to mature and it occupies the land, which is one reason why it is not a very profitable crop for the farmer despite the assured procurement price.

q: The 'Green Revolution' in India is associated with the high yielding varieties of:
options: jute and cotton
tea and coffee
wheat and rice
pulses and millets
explanation: The Green Revolution of the 1960s was centred on the high yielding varieties of wheat and rice, which lifted the grain production of the country, and it was accompanied by the irrigation expansion and the fertiliser use.

q: The 'Blue Revolution' in India relates to:
options: the development of the fish production through the modern methods
the high yielding varieties of wheat
the white revolution of the milk
the hybridisation of the plant breeding
explanation: The Blue Revolution refers to the dramatic increase in the fish production through the modern techniques, the deep sea fishing, the fish breeding and the the aquaculture, and it earned India the title of a leading fish producer.

q: The 'White Revolution' in India was associated with:
options: the silver revolution in eggs and poultry
the Operation Flood and the increase in the milk production
the high yielding varieties of rice
the golden fibre revolution in jute
explanation: The White Revolution, led by Dr Verghese Kurien through the Operation Flood, transformed India into the largest producer of milk in the world with the dairy cooperatives of the Amul model.

q: The 'Golden Revolution' in India was achieved in:
options: the horticultural crops like the honey, the fruits and the vegetables
the fish production
the non conventional energy sources
the milk production
explanation: The Golden Revolution of the 1990s related to the horticulture sector, with India emerging as a leading producer of the fruits, the vegetables, the spices and the honey, and it is also called the Revolution of the Horticulture.

q: The 'Silver Revolution' in India relates to:
options: the fish production
the increase in the egg and the poultry production
the honey production
the milk production
explanation: The Silver Revolution refers to the rapid growth of the poultry and the egg production in the country, and the other revolutions of the colours are the green, the white, the blue, the golden and the silver for the eggs and the poultry.

q: The 'Antyodaya Anna Yojana' provides:
options: the mid day meal in the schools
the subsidised credit to the small farmers
the employment guarantee in the rural areas
free foodgrains to the poorest households of the country
explanation: The Antyodaya Anna Yojana, the poorest of the poor component of the Public Distribution System, provides the free foodgrains to the families that are below the poverty line and are the most vulnerable.

q: The 'Minimum Support Price' in India is:
options: the price at which the imports are allowed to enter
the price determined by the Commission for the Agricultural Costs and the Prices for the retail market
the price at which the government assures the procurement from the farmers
the price fixed by the State Governments for the retail sale
explanation: The MSP is the guaranteed price at which the government agencies will procure the crops from the farmers, and the CACP recommends the levels while the procurement is carried out by the FCI, the State agencies and the cooperatives.

q: The 'Net sown area' in the Indian agriculture statistics is the area:
options: sown with the crops and the land left fallow for a short time is included in it
sown with the crops more than once a year
covered by the forests and the wastelands
irrigated at least once during the year
explanation: The net sown area is the area sown with the crops once or more during the year with the area left fallow for less than a year included in it, and the gross sown area is the sum of the areas sown for the different crops in the year.

q: The 'canal' irrigation system in India is the largest in:
options: the Deccan plateau
the coastal areas of the west
the northern plain
the coastal areas of the east
explanation: The canal system dominates the irrigation of the northern plain where the rivers of the Himalaya and the peninsular rivers feed the extensive canal commands, and the well system is the largest in the Deccan.

q: The 'well irrigation' is the dominant source of irrigation in:
options: the Punjab plains
the Bengal delta
the coastal Andhra
the Deccan plateau
explanation: The wells and the tube wells are the main source of the irrigation in the hard rock of the Deccan plateau because the percolation of the water is easier there, while the Punjab and the Bengal depend on the canals.

q: The 'Per Drop More Crop' programme under the PMKSY aims at:
options: the diversification of the cropping pattern in the rain fed areas
the promotion of the water use efficiency through the drip and the sprinkler irrigation
the increase in the number of the lift irrigation projects
the deepening of the wells in the hard rock
explanation: The Per Drop More Crop component of the PMKSY promotes the micro irrigation to improve the water use efficiency, while the Watershed Development Component works in the rain fed areas and the AIBP covers the command area development.

q: The 'Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure' scheme of the agriculture ministry provides support for:
options: the seed multiplication in the wheat belt
the cold storages, the reefer vans and the primary processing centres for the horticulture produce
the mechanisation of the harvesting in the paddy fields
the marketing of the milk cooperative
explanation: The scheme finances the cold chain and the value addition infrastructure for the perishables like the fruits, the vegetables and the milk so that the wastage of the produce is reduced.

q: The 'National Horticulture Mission' aims at:
options: the procurement of the wheat for the buffer stock
the raising of the foodgrain yield of the rice
the enhancement of the horticulture production and the productivity with the post harvest management
the promotion of the tea and the coffee exports
explanation: The NHM was launched in 2005-06 for the holistic development of the horticulture sector with the area expansion, the productivity improvement, the post harvest management and the market linkage.

q: The 'e-NAM' portal provides the online trading platform for the:
options: the retail vegetable shops in the cities
the export of the gems and the jewellery
the stock exchanges of the corporate sector
the Agricultural Commodities Exchanges of the regulated market yards
explanation: The National Agricultural Market links the agricultural produce market committees of the States on a single online platform so that the buyers and the sellers across the country can trade in the regulated yards.

q: The 'Per capita availability of foodgrains' in India is:
options: higher than the actual consumption because of the stocks and the wastage
lower than the actual consumption
the same as the consumption because of the PDS
low because of the large population of the cattle
explanation: The per capita availability of the foodgrains is around 500 grams a day, which is higher than the actual consumption of about 400 grams, and the difference is explained by the buffer stocks, the exports, the feed and the wastage.

q: The 'Food Security Act' covers:
options: about 75 per cent of the rural and 50 per cent of the urban population
only the families below the poverty line
only the urban poor of the notified cities
the whole of the population without any exception
explanation: The National Food Security Act of 2013 covers about 75 per cent of the rural and 50 per cent of the urban population with the entitlements of the foodgrain and the nutrition support.

q: The 'Operation Flood' was based on the:
options: the private sector dairies of the south
Amul model of the dairy cooperatives
the urban milk supply of the metropolitan cities
the government owned dairy farms
explanation: The Operation Flood was modelled on the Amul cooperative of Anand in Gujarat, and it linked the producer cooperatives with the urban consumers through a network of the dairy cooperatives across the country.

q: The 'spices' in India are grown in the:
options: the black soil of the Deccan only
the alluvial soil of the Punjab
warm and humid climate with the coastal and the laterite soils
the cold arid climate of Ladakh
explanation: The spices need a warm and humid climate and a well drained soil rich in the humus, and the Malabar coast of Kerala, the coastal Karnataka and the Tamil Nadu are the principal producing areas.

q: The 'Krishi Vigyan Kendra' is:
options: a research institute of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for the basic research
a body of the Ministry of Finance for the credit support to the farmers
a university department of the agricultural economics
a farm science centre of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research that provides the extension services to the farmers
explanation: The Krishi Vigyan Kendras are the agricultural extension centres of the ICAR that translate the research into the practice for the farmers through the training and the demonstrations at the district level.

q: The 'Indian Council of Agricultural Research' is:
options: a division of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries
a research wing of the Indian Council of Medical Research
a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament
an autonomous organisation under the Department of Agricultural Research and Education of the Ministry of Agriculture
explanation: The ICAR is the premier research organisation of the country for the agricultural research, and it is an autonomous organisation under the Department of Agricultural Research and Education with its headquarters in New Delhi.

q: The 'The Food Corporation of India' was set up in:
explanation: The FCI was set up in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act to undertake the procurement, the storage, the transportation and the distribution of the foodgrains on behalf of the central and the State governments.

q: The 'The Commission for Price Fixing of Agricultural Commodities' recommends:
options: the minimum support price, the procurement price and the price of the essential commodities
the export duty on the agricultural produce
the crop insurance premium
the interest rate of the agricultural credit
explanation: The CACP under the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare recommends the minimum support price, the procurement price and the price of the essential commodities, and it also advises on the issues of the costs and the prices of the agricultural commodities.

q: The 'farm mechanisation' in India is promoted through the:
options: the Department of Atomic Energy
the Sub-Mission on Mechanisation under the Ministry of Agriculture
the National Capital Region Planning Board
the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
explanation: The Sub-Mission on Mechanisation provides the subsidies for the custom hiring centres and the individual machinery and the equipment to the farmers, and the high level of the mechanisation in the wheat and the rice is credited to it.
